WorldWideWeb browser and the first website (CERN)

Tim Berners-Lee’s first browser and the CERN project page it displayed: the unstyled hypertext that web brutalism looks back to.

Source
CERN, WorldWideWeb browser rebuild (2019)
Creator
Tim Berners-Lee, CERN
Made
1990–1991 (browser and first pages); 2019 (CERN rebuild in a modern browser)
Style
Brutalist web design (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Plain, utilitarian
Evidence
Opened Wikimedia Commons “W3 First Website.png” (1366 × 655 px, uploaded 8 November 2021) with the Read tool on 2026-10-02. It shows the first project page, info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html, in CERN’s 2019 browser rebuild, not on original NeXT hardware. Also viewed “WorldWideWeb.1.png” (834 × 642 px), a screenshot of the original NeXTSTEP application’s panels.
Reviewed
2 October 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

This is a lineage reference. The page was plain because early HTML had no styling, not by choice. Its sans-serif rendering comes from NeXTSTEP, not from later browser defaults.

Context

Smashing Magazine (2020) names the first website as the first example of raw-HTML brutalism.

Commons tags both screenshots as public domain because “the whole project was released into the public domain in 1993”, citing CERN document record 1164399. That record was behind a bot check on 2026-10-02 and was not read. The NeXTSTEP screenshot itself shows “Copyright 1990,91,93,94, TBL, CERN. Distribution restricted: ask for terms.”

Observed

  • In the rebuild, a white document window with a black title bar sits on a dark gray desktop beside a gray menu column (Info, Navigate, Document, Edit, Links, Style, Print).
  • The page has a bold, centered sans-serif heading, “World Wide Web”, and two indented paragraphs of black text.
  • Below them, a two-column list pairs underlined link titles (What’s out there?, Help, Software Products, Technical, Bibliography) with plain descriptions.
  • Links are black and underlined. There is no color, image, rule, or box on the page.

Why it belongs

The first page already shows the core of Brutalist web design: structure carried only by headings, paragraphs, lists, and underlines. Blue links came later, with browsers such as NCSA Mosaic.

Borrow

Write link text that says where the link goes, and put a one-line plain description next to it.
